introduction.p: These problems compare numerical integration rules, finite-difference derivatives, and Newton iteration. For each approximation, identify the exact quantity, the algorithm, its hypotheses, and the available error evidence.

subsection.title: Chapter map

cell.p: Midpoint rule
Replace the graph on each subinterval by a midpoint rectangle.
The second derivative, through curvature.
Trapezoidal rule
Replace the graph on each subinterval by a secant line.
The second derivative, through curvature.
Simpson’s Rule
Replace the graph on pairs of subintervals by a parabola.
The fourth derivative, because Simpson is exact through cubics.
Finite differences
Replace a derivative limit by a quotient with small nonzero step h.
Truncation error and roundoff error.
Newton’s method
Replace the graph near a guess by its tangent line.
The starting point, the derivative near the root, and the multiplicity of the root.

subsection.p: The error estimates have hypotheses. Those hypotheses are not decoration. The midpoint and trapezoidal bounds need a bounded second derivative. Simpson’s bound needs a bounded fourth derivative. Newton’s fast convergence needs a simple root and a good starting point. Numerical differentiation is sensitive to roundoff because it subtracts nearly equal numbers.
A method can still produce a number when its hypotheses fail. The guarantee is what may fail.

exercise.title: What common idea unites the chapter’s methods?

statement.p: Midpoint, trapezoid, Simpson, finite differences, and Newton’s method all replace a difficult object by a simpler local picture. In your own words, what is that common idea, and why is controlling the error as important as producing the approximation?

hint.p: Local information can produce global understanding only if we know how large the replacement error might be.

exercise.title: What is the difference between a method producing a number and a theorem guaranteeing accuracy?

statement.p: A numerical rule can still return a decimal when its error-bound hypotheses fail. In your own words, what exactly fails in that situation, and why should stabilization of a table not be confused with a proof?

hint.p: The guarantee is what may fail, not necessarily the approximation. Close successive values are evidence, not a theorem.

exercise.title: What extra discipline does Newton’s method need as an algorithm?

statement.p: The tangent-line idea is simple, but the computational version asks when to stop and whether the root is simple. In your own words, why should both residual and step size be monitored, and what does linear rather than quadratic convergence suggest?

hint.p: A small residual or a small step can each mislead. Slow convergence may mean a multiple root or a bad starting point.

exercise.title: Why is numerical integration usually more forgiving than numerical differentiation?

statement.p: Integration averages values over an interval. Differentiation subtracts nearby values and divides by a small step. In your own words, why do those two personalities lead to different computational warnings?

hint.p: Averaging can reduce noise. Subtracting nearly equal values and dividing by a small step magnifies roundoff and measurement noise. For a sufficiently smooth function, shrinking the step reduces truncation error, so these competing errors require a balance.

note.title: End-of-chapter habit
note.p: For every numerical answer, ask four questions:

p.me: \text{What evidence or theorem supports the claimed accuracy?}

subsection.p: The next section turns this habit toward a new kind of problem. So far, numerical methods have mostly produced numbers: values of integrals, derivatives, and roots. But many laws of science ask for more than one number. They ask for a whole unknown function.
